title: Russian Federation: Authorities impose censorship on media and crush peaceful anti-war protests following invasion of Ukraine
claim: Roskomnadzor effectively ordered media to rely only on official Russian sources about the invasion and threatened sanctions for reporting from other sources.
source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Amnesty statement published four days after the invasion with direct policy description.
period_fit: Immediate post-invasion domestic information-control evidence for 2022.
ruler_attribution: Attributable to Putin's presidency and the Russian state's censorship apparatus.
contrary_evidence: The statement reports the official rationale but does not validate it.

title: Russia: Kremlin’s ruthless crackdown stifles independent journalism and anti-war movement
claim: Amnesty said Russia had blocked independent media, banned Facebook and Twitter, and arbitrarily arrested more than 13,800 people at anti-war rallies since 24 February 2022.
source_confidence_reason: Direct 2022 field summary with an explicit arrest count and named restrictions.
period_fit: Covers the first two weeks of the full-scale war and its domestic repression response.
ruler_attribution: The crackdown was carried out by Russian authorities under Putin.
contrary_evidence: The arrest figure is a monitoring estimate, not an official government total.

title: Russia Criminalizes Independent War Reporting, Anti-War Protests
claim: HRW said Putin signed laws on 4 March 2022 that criminalized independent war reporting and anti-war protest, with penalties of up to 15 years in prison.
source_confidence_reason: Specific law-adoption dates and penalties are named in a contemporaneous HRW report.
period_fit: Directly within the 2022 domestic repression wave.
ruler_attribution: The laws were signed by Putin and enforced by his state institutions.
contrary_evidence: The government framed the laws as anti-disinformation measures.

title: More than 4,300 detained at anti-war protests in Russia
claim: Reuters reporting republished by Euronews said police detained more than 4,300 people at anti-war protests across Russia and that one protester was shown beaten on the ground by riot police.
source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous Reuters-reported protest tally with concrete police-violence detail.
ruler_attribution: The detentions were carried out by Russian police under Putin's government.
contrary_evidence: Reuters noted it could not independently verify some social-media footage.

title: Russia: Freedom on the Net 2022 Country Report
claim: Freedom House reported that Russia blocked more than 5,000 websites after the invasion, expanded state blocking powers, and deepened self-censorship around war, corruption, and LGBT topics.
source_confidence_reason: Detailed country report with explicit 2022 findings and explanatory text.
ruler_attribution: These were state actions under Putin's rule, primarily through Roskomnadzor and allied agencies.
contrary_evidence: The report also notes broad internet access remained widespread, so the issue is control and censorship rather than total shutdown.

title: Russia: Authorities deploy new criminal laws to silence criticism of Russia’s war in Ukraine
claim: Amnesty said people were already being detained in 2022 for public criticism of the war, and that the new criminal laws were incompatible with freedom of expression.
source_confidence_reason: Directly contemporaneous with the wartime legal crackdown and explicitly tied to detentions.
ruler_attribution: The laws and detentions were under Putin's authority.
contrary_evidence: The statement is advocacy-based and does not itself adjudicate every individual case.

title: Russian journalists are being silenced to stifle reporting of protests
claim: Amnesty said the Russian authorities used severe reprisals, arbitrary arrests, force, detentions, and heavy fines to crush public protest and suppress reporting by journalists and monitors.
source_confidence_reason: Focused 2022 report with clear domestic-safety implications and detailed methods of repression.
ruler_attribution: The suppression is attributable to Russian state authorities under Putin.
contrary_evidence: The report also notes the anti-war movement still generated protests despite the crackdown.

title: We publish a report on political prisoners and political repression in Russia in 2022
claim: Memorial said political prisoners in Russia reached 513 by the end of 2022 and described the year as a turning point for harsher repression.
source_confidence_reason: Specialized political-prisoner monitoring project summarizing its 2022 annual report with explicit counts.
ruler_attribution: The political repression occurred under Putin's state system.
contrary_evidence: The figure is an incomplete list and therefore a conservative count.

title: Russia: Authorities impose censorship on media and crush peaceful anti-war protests following invasion of Ukraine
claim: Amnesty described the censorship order as part of a broader effort that also crushed peaceful anti-war protests and dissent.
source_confidence_reason: Same source, distinct passage linking censorship to protest suppression.
ruler_attribution: The broader repression was carried out by Russian authorities under Putin.
contrary_evidence: This is a civil-liberties source, not a criminal court finding.

title: World Report 2023: Russian Federation
claim: HRW reported that torture and ill-treatment by law-enforcement officials persisted in 2022, including beatings, electroshock, waterboarding allegations, and punishment cells for Navalny and Yuri Dmitriyev.
source_confidence_reason: Annual report with specific 2022 incidents, official in time for 2022 conduct assessment.
period_fit: Covers March to October 2022 domestic policing and prison abuse.
ruler_attribution: These abuses occurred under Putin's security and prison system.
contrary_evidence: The report describes specific incidents and allegations; it does not claim all custody abuse was centrally directed in each case.

title: World Report 2022: Russia
claim: HRW said authorities regularly let torture, ill-treatment, and suspicious deaths in custody go unpunished, and documented Chechen abductions, anti-LGBT attacks, and failures to investigate domestic violence and police misconduct.
source_confidence_reason: Annual rights report with a broad, well-specified baseline for inherited and continuing abuse.
ruler_attribution: These are national-level abuses and failures under Putin's rule; some Chechnya conduct is by Kadyrov's local apparatus but with federal responsibility issues raised in the report.
contrary_evidence: Some abuses are regional or locally executed, so attribution to Putin is indirect rather than always immediate.

title: Правозащитные организации обратились к Владимиру Путину по факту похищения родственников критиков главы Чечни
claim: A coalition of rights groups told Putin that dozens of relatives of Chechen critics had been abducted, their whereabouts were unknown, and the acts appeared to be enforced disappearances carried out by state-linked forces.
source_confidence_reason: Direct 2022 letter to Putin with specific victims, alleged methods, and responsibility claims.
period_fit: Immediately before the 2022 invasion, showing inherited domestic coercion in Russia's federation.
ruler_attribution: The letter explicitly assigns federal responsibility to Putin as president and guarantor of rights.
contrary_evidence: The underlying facts concern Chechnya and some details were still being clarified at the time.

title: World Report 2022: Russia
claim: HRW said Russia's government continued anti-LGBT discrimination and failed to investigate threats and attacks against LGBT people, and that domestic violence remained a systemic failure with poor police response and inadequate shelters.
source_confidence_reason: The report ties 2022 domestic protection failures to named vulnerable groups and institutional omissions.
period_fit: Baseline into 2022 and continuing through the year.
ruler_attribution: These are national-level protection failures under Putin's government, not just private harms.
contrary_evidence: Some incidents are local and some victims left the country, so the report is a pattern-level source rather than a total tally.

title: Russia: Expanded 'Gay Propaganda' Ban Progresses Toward Law
claim: HRW said the State Duma backed legislation that would further restrict LGBT expression, including positive or neutral information about LGBT people, with hefty fines and broader stigmatization.
source_confidence_reason: Clear late-2022 legislative analysis with legal and rights implications spelled out.
period_fit: Late 2022 domestic vulnerability and incitement environment.
ruler_attribution: This legislative trajectory occurred under Putin and his ruling coalition.
contrary_evidence: Lawmakers said they were defending morality and 'traditional values'.

title: Russia's parliament passes law banning 'LGBT propaganda' among adults
claim: Reuters reported that Russia expanded its LGBT-propaganda ban to all ages, with fines and possible arrest for foreigners, in a move critics said was meant to intimidate and oppress sexual minorities.
source_confidence_reason: Reuters-reported legislative coverage with direct details on scope and penalties.
period_fit: Exactly within 2022 and directly relevant to vulnerable-group protection.
ruler_attribution: The law was being pushed and would be signed under Putin's authority.
contrary_evidence: The government framed it as a morality and child-protection measure.

title: ‘The purification of society will only strengthen the country’ Meduza’s brief retelling of Putin’s darkest speech yet
claim: Meduza reported that Putin publicly denounced a 'fifth column' of 'traitors' and praised 'purification of society,' while claiming Russia was forced into war and that troops were avoiding civilian casualties.
source_confidence_reason: Directly reports a specific Putin speech with language relevant to incitement and fear climate.
ruler_attribution: The rhetoric is directly attributable to Putin.
contrary_evidence: The article is a retelling rather than a Kremlin transcript.

title: Factbox: Memorial, chronicler of Soviet and recent crimes, banned by Putin
claim: Reuters-reported coverage said Russia ordered Memorial dissolved in 2021, capping a year of crackdowns on Kremlin critics and removing a key civil-society watchdog from the domestic accountability landscape.
source_confidence_reason: Reuters factbox hosted by Euronews with direct explanation of Memorial's dissolution and function.
period_fit: Inherited repression baseline relevant to 2022 accountability and remedy.
ruler_attribution: The dissolution occurred under Putin's rule and affected domestic oversight capacity.
contrary_evidence: The source is a factbox about Memorial, not a formal legal finding about each prosecution it handled.

title: Москва | Human Rights Center MEMORIAL
claim: Memorial's Moscow region page listed ongoing 2022 political-prisoner cases, including Navalny associates, journalists, and other defendants, showing continued tracking of politically motivated prosecutions.
source_confidence_reason: Direct case-listing page with dated 2022 entries, though it is a rolling case docket rather than a single report.
ruler_attribution: These prosecutions occurred under Putin's state apparatus.
contrary_evidence: It is a case registry, so the page reflects Memorial's selection and updating rather than a closed annual count.

title: Положение политических заключенных в России
claim: Memorial's joint submission reported that the general political-prisoner list had grown sharply, from 46 in 2018 to 141 by 5 April 2023, with a separate religious list of 410, illustrating the scale of repression carried through 2022 and beyond.
source_confidence_reason: Specialized human-rights dossier with explicit list counts, though the page is a 2023 submission about a longer trend.
period_fit: Trendline that brackets the 2022 repression environment.
ruler_attribution: The growth of political imprisonment occurred under Putin's rule.
contrary_evidence: The page is a later submission and includes a broader period than just 2022.

title: Russia: More than 1,300 protesters detained after Putin's partial military draft
claim: Amnesty said at least 1,386 peaceful protesters were detained across Russia after Putin's partial mobilization call, and police used unnecessary and excessive force including beatings and chokeholds; some detainees also faced summons to enlistment centres.
source_confidence_reason: Contemporaneous human-rights reporting with a concrete detention count and detailed policing description; strong for the repression mechanism, though based on Amnesty and OVD-Info reporting rather than direct state admission.
ruler_attribution: High: the crackdown followed Putin's mobilization call and was enforced by state police under his government.
contrary_evidence: Russian authorities treated anti-mobilization protests as unlawful and framed mobilization as necessary for the war effort.

title: Human Rights Committee Considers Report of the Russian Federation in the Absence of a Delegation, Experts Raise Issues on the Persecution of Journalists and the Arrests of Protesters
claim: Committee experts said there had been thousands of cases of harassment and persecution of journalists, dozens of murders and attempted murders, journalists abducted and tortured, hundreds of Russian journalists detained for reporting on the war or protests, and mass arrests in response to peaceful demonstrations.
source_confidence_reason: Official UN meeting summary of treaty-body review with direct expert statements and concrete allegations; strong independent corroboration of repression patterns.
ruler_attribution: High: the discussion concerned conduct by Russian authorities and Russian forces during Putin's 2022 rule.
contrary_evidence: Russian officials and aligned media disputed the scale and legitimacy of the allegations.

title: Human Rights Committee Considers Report of the Russian Federation in the Absence of a Delegation, Experts Raise Issues on the Persecution of Journalists and the Arrests of Protesters
claim: Committee experts said reports since February 2022 included excessive force, extrajudicial executions, torture, rape and sexual violence, forced conscription of civilians, and in September 2022 the detention and beating of 20 women who protested the conscription of Chechens; they also described serious and continuous violations and widespread impunity in Chechnya and anti-LGBT violence in the North Caucasus.
source_confidence_reason: Official UN expert summary with specific examples, victim groups, and attribution to Russian-controlled or tolerated conduct; strong for domestic safety and vulnerable-group abuse.
ruler_attribution: High: the conduct was described as occurring under Russian state or tolerated regional authority within Putin's federal system, including conscription enforcement and Chechnya-related abuses.
contrary_evidence: Russian authorities denied or minimized such allegations and presented the cases as lawful security or morality enforcement.

title: Submission by Human Rights Watch on Russia to the Human Rights Committee
claim: Human Rights Watch told the Human Rights Committee that Russian authorities had integrated facial-recognition systems with public surveillance to identify and prosecute peaceful protesters, and that domestic courts had dismissed challenges, leaving no effective remedy for the rights violations.
source_confidence_reason: Specialist human-rights submission with a specific technology-and-policing mechanism and explicit legal-remedy failure; strong but still an advocacy submission.
ruler_attribution: Moderate to high: the surveillance system was a state policing choice under Putin's government, though the cited examples include Moscow-level enforcement rather than a presidential order.
contrary_evidence: The report notes Russian courts rejected the challenges, which is a state justification rather than independent validation of legality.

title: Submission by Human Rights Watch on Russia to the Human Rights Committee
claim: Human Rights Watch told the Human Rights Committee that Chechen authorities used arbitrary detention, torture, collective punishment and public humiliation against perceived undesirables, including the January 2022 abduction of Zarema Mussaeva, and it called on Russia to stop these abuses and hold responsible officials to account.
source_confidence_reason: Detailed human-rights submission with concrete cases and a direct accountability appeal; strong for a recurring regional abuse mechanism, though attribution is partly via tolerance and failure to prevent.
period_fit: Directly in-period, including January 2022 and the 2022 submission date.
ruler_attribution: Moderate to high: Chechen abuses are not identical to a presidential order, but they occurred inside Putin's political system amid long-running impunity and feasible higher-level intervention.
contrary_evidence: The Russian state did not acknowledge a systemic abuse problem and publicly treated Chechen security actions as internal law-enforcement matters.
